paragraphs: Expectation maximization, or EM, supports learning when a model involves quantities that are not directly observed, such as missing observations or hidden mixture assignments. Its expectation step computes conditional expectations, while its maximization step updates the model. With a large training set, repeatedly evaluating conditional expectations across all examples can become a substantial computational burden.

The paper introduces SPIDER-EM, which adapts the stochastic path integral differential estimator to approximate the full conditional expectation used in the expectation step. The central change concerns how this quantity is estimated. This gives the authors a way to analyze the cost of conditional expectation calculations separately from the number of maximization steps.

For smooth, nonconvex likelihoods, the authors establish finite-time bounds for reaching an epsilon-approximate stationary point. The maximization-step count scales as O(1/epsilon), while per-example conditional expectation evaluations scale as n plus sqrt(n) times O(1/epsilon). These bounds improve on the compared algorithms, and numerical results support the analysis. The guarantee concerns approximate stationarity, rather than finding a global optimum.
neurips-2020-a-stochastic-path-integral-.tldr: SPIDER-EM reduces the conditional expectation work needed to reach an approximate stationary point in large-data EM problems.

paragraphs: Time series forecasting must account for variability in future observations and for errors that can compound over a long forecast. The paper highlights a training-to-inference mismatch in autoregressive prediction: training uses observed previous values, whereas inference feeds the model its own earlier predictions. Errors can therefore become inputs to subsequent predictions.

The proposed Adversarial Sparse Transformer, or AST, combines a Sparse Transformer generator with a discriminator. The generator learns a sparse attention map for forecasting, giving the model a learned pattern of connections within the sequence. The discriminator contributes a sequence-level training signal, so prediction quality is assessed across a sequence rather than only through individual forecast values.

This design brings sparse attention and adversarial learning together to address the forecasting problems identified by the authors. Experiments on several real-world datasets report that AST is effective and efficient. Those findings support the combined approach in the evaluated settings; the abstract does not establish that accumulated prediction errors disappear or that every future outcome is captured.
neurips-2020-adversarial-sparse-transfor.tldr: AST combines learned sparse attention with sequence-level adversarial training to improve time series forecasting.

paragraphs: A regression model can predict a numerical value while also expressing uncertainty about that prediction. The paper addresses the reliability of this uncertainty: deep neural networks can be overconfident, making their reported confidence a poor guide to their actual errors. Its objective is to produce predictions whose uncertainty better matches observed outcomes.

The proposed method uses maximum mean discrepancy, a measure based on representing distributions through a kernel. Calibration is pursued by minimizing this kernel-based discrepancy. This makes the agreement underlying calibrated uncertainty part of the learning objective, rather than evaluating a model solely by the accuracy of its central numerical predictions.

The authors prove that the method's calibration error approaches zero asymptotically as the sample size becomes sufficiently large. This is a large-sample result, rather than a promise of exact calibration on any finite dataset. Experiments on real datasets produce prediction intervals that are both well calibrated and sharp, meaning informative rather than unnecessarily broad. The reported comparisons outperform related state-of-the-art methods.
neurips-2020-calibrated-reliable-regress.tldr: A kernel-based discrepancy objective improves regression uncertainty, with asymptotic calibration guarantees and strong empirical prediction intervals.

paragraphs: Some networks are observed as interactions with timestamps rather than as a single fixed collection of connections. Messages between people and transactions between traders are examples. The paper introduces Community Hawkes Independent Pairs, or CHIP, as a generative model for these continuous-time networks, linking the modeling of relational events with the identification of communities.

For community detection, the authors construct an aggregated adjacency matrix from the model and apply spectral clustering. They prove consistency as both the number of nodes and the observation duration grow. They also develop parameter estimators that are consistent and computationally efficient. These results provide theoretical support for recovering structure and estimating the model in the stated growing-data setting.

The empirical results address whether the approach remains useful at substantial network sizes. CHIP and its estimation procedure handle networks containing tens of thousands of nodes. On several real networks, they also provide better fits than existing continuous-time network models. Together, these findings connect statistical estimation guarantees with demonstrated computational scalability and improved descriptions of observed interaction data.
neurips-2020-chip-a-hawkes-process-model.tldr: CHIP models timestamped network interactions with scalable estimation and consistency guarantees for community detection and model parameters.

paragraphs: Image restoration networks often process information at several resolutions, but deciding how to connect those resolutions typically requires manual architecture design. CLEARER automates this process through a search space tailored to restoration. Its aim is to discover useful ways to extract and combine multi-resolution features while considering the tradeoff between model complexity and performance.

The search space has three modules. Parallel modules maintain processing at multiple resolutions; transition modules retain existing features while adding a lower resolution; fusion modules combine information across parallel branches. These building blocks make the timing and arrangement of multi-resolution processing explicit architectural choices that the search can adjust.

The authors also introduce losses that balance complexity against performance and encourage continuous architecture parameters toward values near zero or one. This enables differentiable search while easing the conversion to discrete choices. CLEARER can find a promising architecture in two GPU hours. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report promising results against nine denoising methods and eight deraining approaches, supporting its use for automatically designing restoration networks.
neurips-2020-clearer-multi-scale-neural-.tldr: CLEARER searches how image restoration networks process and combine multiple resolutions while balancing performance and model complexity.

paragraphs: Combining reinforcement learning with search has been successful in settings where an agent can observe the relevant game state. Hidden information creates a further challenge, and the paper identifies that earlier algorithms in this tradition cannot handle imperfect-information games. ReBeL extends the combination of self-play learning and search to this setting.

The framework has a convergence guarantee to a Nash equilibrium in any two-player zero-sum game. Such an equilibrium describes strategies for which neither player can benefit by changing their strategy alone. In perfect-information games, ReBeL reduces to an algorithm resembling AlphaZero, connecting the framework to an established approach while extending its scope to games with hidden information.

Experiments in two imperfect-information games show convergence to approximate Nash equilibria. The authors also report superhuman performance in heads-up no-limit Texas hold'em poker while using substantially less domain knowledge than previous poker AI. The theoretical result and empirical findings play distinct roles: one establishes the framework's convergence property, while the others demonstrate approximate equilibrium behavior and strong play in specific games.
neurips-2020-combining-deep-reinforcemen.tldr: ReBeL combines self-play reinforcement learning and search for imperfect-information games, with equilibrium guarantees and superhuman heads-up poker performance.

paragraphs: Explaining a neuron with a single concept label can miss much of what activates it. This paper instead searches for logical combinations of concepts that approximate a neuron's behavior. Compositional explanations offer a more expressive description, allowing the analysis to capture both coherent abstractions and neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features.

The authors apply the procedure to image classification and natural language inference. In vision, they find many neurons representing abstract but semantically coherent concepts, alongside polysemantic neurons that detect unrelated features. In natural language inference, they find neurons using shallow word-based heuristics associated with dataset biases. The explanations therefore reveal different kinds of learned behavior across the two settings.

The paper also relates these patterns to performance. Human-interpretable visual concepts correlate positively with task performance, while shallow language heuristics correlate negatively; these are associations rather than causal claims. Finally, the authors show that end users can use the explanations to construct simple copy-paste adversarial examples that alter model behavior predictably, making the explanations useful for probing model responses.
neurips-2020-compositional-explanations-.tldr: Logical combinations of concepts explain neuron behavior more expressively and reveal patterns associated with performance and predictable adversarial responses.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds visual representations from unlabeled images by comparing augmented examples. Positive pairs come from different augmentations of the same example, while negative pairs provide contrasts with other examples. The paper focuses on how to make these comparisons more challenging, particularly the negative pairs that earlier approaches did not explicitly select jointly across a batch.

The proposed method, CLAE, introduces adversarial examples designed for contrastive learning and uses them in a self-supervised adversarial training algorithm. The adversarial examples create more difficult positive pairs. By considering all images in the batch during optimization, the training procedure also produces harder negative pairs, making the relationships among examples part of the challenge construction.

This approach matters because it changes how demanding the learning task is without requiring labeled training examples. CLAE is compatible with many existing contrastive learning methods, allowing it to augment several established approaches. Experiments on multiple datasets show performance improvements over several standard contrastive learning baselines, providing empirical support for constructing challenging pairs through adversarial optimization.
neurips-2020-contrastive-learning-with-a.tldr: CLAE improves self-supervised contrastive learning by constructing harder positive and negative pairs through adversarial optimization.

paragraphs: Private inference uses cryptographic techniques to process a client's input without disclosing it. The paper identifies inference latency as a major obstacle and argues that conventional neural network architectures are poorly matched to this setting. An architecture that is efficient under ordinary computation may allocate work badly when cryptographic processing changes which operations are expensive.

CryptoNAS centers architecture search on that changed cost structure. In the private inference setting described, nonlinear operations such as ReLU dominate latency, while linear layers are effectively free by comparison. The authors therefore use a ReLU budget as a proxy for latency and search for models that maximize accuracy while staying within that budget.

The reported results improve accuracy by 3.4% and latency by a factor of 2.4 over the state of the art. These findings support tailoring architecture search to the costs of private inference, rather than assuming ordinary efficiency measures transfer directly. The budget is a latency proxy: its role is to guide model design toward the operations that matter most in this computational setting.
neurips-2020-cryptonas-private-inference.tldr: CryptoNAS improves private inference by searching for accurate networks under a budget on costly ReLU operations.

paragraphs: Graph neural network research often evaluates individual architectures on particular tasks. This paper instead organizes architecture choices into a shared design space, including dimensions such as layer count and aggregation function. The resulting space contains 315,000 designs, which the authors systematically study across 32 predictive tasks using an efficient evaluation approach.

The work also defines a task space with a similarity measure. Its purpose is to help identify which architecture choices may transfer to a new task or dataset. This addresses the authors' finding that the strongest designs vary considerably across tasks: useful architectural guidance needs to account for the task rather than simply select one universally preferred design.

The study produces design guidelines, demonstrates transfer of strong designs across tasks, and discovers models achieving state-of-the-art performance. The authors also release GraphGym, a platform combining modular implementations, standardized evaluation, and reproducible experiment management. Together, the framework and platform support studying relationships between architecture and task at a broader scale than isolated model comparisons.
neurips-2020-design-space-for-graph-neur.tldr: A systematic study of GNN architectures and task similarity yields design guidelines, transferable architecture choices, and the GraphGym platform.

paragraphs: For cross-entropy and related classification losses, minimizing weights can lie infinitely far away. That makes convergence of weight values an awkward description of learning. This paper shows that weights trained by gradient flow can nevertheless converge in direction, with predictions, training errors, and the distribution of classification margins converging as consequences.

The proof applies to deep homogeneous networks, a class allowing ReLU, max-pooling, linear, and convolutional layers. It requires perfect classification accuracy but imposes no requirements on network width or initialization. The authors provide empirical support both in networks close to the theoretical setting and in non-homogeneous networks, keeping that experimental evidence distinct from the proved scope.

An additional result assumes locally Lipschitz gradients. Under that condition, gradients also converge in direction and eventually align with the gradient flow path, yielding consequences for margin maximization and saliency-map convergence. The analysis develops tools for unbounded, nonsmooth functions and offers a perspective distinct from neural tangent and mean-field theories: training can stabilize in meaningful ways even while weight magnitudes keep growing.
neurips-2020-directional-convergence-and.tldr: Under the stated conditions, gradient flow stabilizes network weight directions and predictions even when minimizing weight magnitudes diverge.

paragraphs: An agent with limited memory resources must decide which information deserves a precise representation. This paper frames that decision as part of reward maximization. It assigns a cost to accurately storing action-values, allowing different memories to have different precision, so the agent must balance the usefulness of an estimate against the resources needed to maintain it.

From this formulation, the authors derive Dynamic Resource Allocator, or DRA. They apply it to two reinforcement learning tasks and a model-based planning task. DRA devotes more resources to memories with greater influence on cumulative rewards, giving a principled account of why some remembered values should be represented more accurately than others.

DRA also learns faster when its initial resource budget exceeds the amount it eventually allocates to perform well. The authors suggest this may help explain stronger early engagement of frontal cortical areas during learning, rather than establishing a biological mechanism. More broadly, the framework supplies an adaptive solution for distributing costly resources among uncertain memories as the environment changes.
neurips-2020-dynamic-allocation-of-limit.tldr: DRA learns how to distribute limited memory precision toward action-values that matter most for cumulative reward.

paragraphs: Unsupervised and self-supervised learning often improve representations used for later prediction tasks, but explaining their benefits theoretically remains difficult. This paper presents a common perspective: several such methods use unlabeled data and a learnable function to regularize the representation. That function restricts which representations are considered suitable before or alongside learning the downstream prediction task.

The authors build a discriminative framework for analyzing sample complexity, meaning how much labeled data learning requires. Their bounds show that learnable regularization can prune the hypothesis space when the chosen classes of functions exploit the data's structure. The benefit is conditional on those choices; the theory does not say that any auxiliary objective automatically reduces label requirements.

Two examples make the framework concrete: auto-encoder-based regularization and masked self-supervision. For each, the authors quantify a reduction in the labeled-data sample complexity bound. Complementary experiments support the analysis. The contribution is a shared theoretical language for understanding how useful constraints learned from unlabeled examples can narrow the downstream learning problem.
neurips-2020-functional-regularization-f.tldr: A unified theory shows how suitably chosen learnable regularization from unlabeled data can reduce downstream labeled-data requirements.

paragraphs: Probabilistic neural networks commonly give each weight an independent prior. Such priors do not express correlations among weights and provide a limited interface for specifying desired behavior of the resulting function. This paper seeks a more structured way to encode relationships among weights and knowledge such as periodicity or dependence on the input context.

The first contribution is a hierarchical model that uses Gaussian processes and unit priors to represent correlated weight structures. The second extends these weight priors to depend on inputs. Kernels defined over contextual inputs then offer a way to regularize the functions represented by the network, connecting assumptions about behavior to the probability model over weights.

The authors demonstrate desirable uncertainty estimates on out-of-distribution test data. They also present cases where kernel-based inductive biases help both interpolation within the training-data region and extrapolation beyond it. These findings support structured priors as a practical interface for expressing functional assumptions, while the reported benefits remain demonstrations in particular cases rather than universal guarantees of calibrated uncertainty.
neurips-2020-hierarchical-gaussian-proce.tldr: Hierarchical Gaussian process priors encode correlated and input-dependent neural network weights to express functional assumptions and improve demonstrated uncertainty behavior.

paragraphs: Generating speech waveforms requires both convincing audio quality and efficient computation. Earlier GAN-based methods offered sampling and memory advantages but had not matched the quality of autoregressive and flow-based alternatives. HiFi-GAN addresses this gap, with the paper emphasizing the importance of modeling periodic patterns arising from speech's sinusoidal components.

On a single-speaker dataset, subjective human ratings indicate quality similar to human speech. The model generates 22.05 kHz audio at 167.9 times real-time speed on one V100 GPU. These are complementary findings: the listening evaluation addresses perceived quality, while the generation measurement establishes speed under the reported hardware and audio setting.

The authors also demonstrate mel-spectrogram inversion for unseen speakers and use in end-to-end speech synthesis, extending the evidence beyond the single-speaker evaluation. A smaller version generates audio at 13.4 times real-time speed on a CPU, with quality comparable to an autoregressive counterpart. Together, the results show that the approach supports different computational footprints while retaining strong demonstrated speech quality.
neurips-2020-hifi-gan-generative-adversa.tldr: HiFi-GAN models periodic audio patterns to combine high-quality speech synthesis with fast generation on GPUs and, in a smaller version, CPUs.

paragraphs: Parallel reinforcement learning systems divide work between actors that collect experience and learners that update the policy. Synchronous designs offer training stability but can limit throughput. Asynchronous designs process more data, yet actors may use outdated policies, creating the stale-policy problem associated with reduced stability and sample efficiency.

High-Throughput Synchronous Deep Reinforcement Learning, or HTS-RL, combines concurrent learning and rollout collection with a system design that avoids stale policies. Actors interact asynchronously with separate environment replicas while the overall system maintains full determinism. The approach therefore reorganizes how collection and learning overlap while retaining the coordination properties sought in synchronous training.

Evaluations use Atari games and the Google Research Football environment. HTS-RL is two to six times faster than synchronous baselines. Against state-of-the-art asynchronous methods, it achieves competitive throughput and consistently higher average episode rewards in the reported comparisons. These results support the system's central goal: improving processing speed while preserving the training benefits that motivate synchronous actor-learner methods.
neurips-2020-high-throughput-synchronous.tldr: HTS-RL overlaps learning and experience collection to accelerate synchronous reinforcement learning while avoiding stale policies.

paragraphs: Training examples can hinder generalization when their labels are wrong or their content is overly ambiguous. This paper introduces a method for detecting problematic examples by observing how they behave during neural network training. Its Area Under the Margin statistic, or AUM, draws on differences in the learning dynamics of clean and mislabeled samples.

To determine a cutoff, the method adds an extra class containing deliberately mislabeled threshold examples. These examples provide a reference for learning an AUM upper bound that isolates suspected mislabeled data. The procedure turns a training-dynamics statistic into a practical selection rule, allowing the influence of problematic examples to be reduced through their removal.

The approach improves on prior work across synthetic and real-world datasets. On WebVision50, removing 17% of training examples yields an absolute 1.6% improvement in test error. On CIFAR100, removing 13% produces a 1.2% error reduction. These results show that retaining more training data is not always beneficial when some labels undermine learning, and that training behavior can help identify such examples.
neurips-2020-identifying-mislabeled-data.tldr: AUM uses training dynamics and deliberately mislabeled reference examples to identify harmful training data and improve test performance.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps users' training inputs on their devices while sharing parameter updates with a server. This paper investigates whether those updates can nevertheless reveal the inputs. Its central finding is that gradients can contain enough information to reconstruct images faithfully, so keeping the original data local does not by itself establish privacy.

The authors combine a loss insensitive to gradient magnitude with optimization strategies drawn from adversarial attacks. They demonstrate high-resolution image reconstruction, including for trained deep networks, extending beyond the contrived settings of earlier attacks. They also study how architecture and parameter choices affect reconstruction difficulty and prove an analytical reconstruction result for inputs to fully connected layers, independent of the remaining architecture.

The paper then examines aggregation settings relevant to practical federated learning. Combining gradients across several images or several training iterations still does not guarantee privacy. This establishes a failure of aggregation as a general assurance, rather than claiming every aggregated update is equally easy to invert. The work shows why shared gradients themselves must be considered a potential source of private information.
neurips-2020-inverting-gradients-how-eas.tldr: Shared gradients can reveal high-resolution training images, and aggregating updates does not guarantee federated learning privacy.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a sampling method for complex continuous distributions, but its usual formulation does not accommodate distributions containing both discrete and continuous variables. Such mixed distributions require a way to update the two kinds of quantities together. This paper introduces mixed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or M-HMC, as a general framework for that purpose.

M-HMC evolves discrete and continuous variables in tandem. This permits more frequent changes to discrete variables while preserving HMC's ability to suppress random-walk behavior, where sampling progresses through less directed wandering. The authors establish theoretical properties of the framework and describe an efficient implementation using Laplace momentum that adds minimal overhead relative to existing HMC methods.

Numerical experiments examine Gaussian mixture models, variable selection in Bayesian logistic regression, and correlated topic models. M-HMC outperforms existing methods in those experiments. The contribution combines a broader sampling framework with an implementation intended to retain computational efficiency, and the reported evaluations demonstrate its usefulness across several models that involve both discrete choices and continuous quantities.
neurips-2020-mixed-hamiltonian-monte-car.tldr: M-HMC jointly updates discrete and continuous variables while retaining HMC's resistance to random-walk sampling behavior.

paragraphs: Online learning requires repeated decisions as losses are encountered over time. This paper considers nonconvex losses and imperfect feedback: at each stage, the learner observes or constructs only an approximate model of the current loss function. The central question is how effectively learning can proceed when neither a simple loss shape nor an exact loss model is available.

The authors propose a mixed-strategy policy based on dual averaging. They derive tight regret guarantees against two comparators: the best fixed decision in hindsight and the best dynamic policy in hindsight. These comparisons assess different goals, since a fixed comparator uses one choice throughout while a dynamic comparator can change its decisions over time.

The framework also covers a more restricted feedback setting in which the learner sees only the loss of the action it actually took. A kernel-based estimator turns these realized losses into approximate models for each round. This connects the general analysis to limited-feedback learning by showing how the inexact models assumed by the policy can be constructed from observed outcomes.
neurips-2020-online-non-convex-optimizat.tldr: A dual-averaging policy provides regret guarantees for online nonconvex learning using approximate loss models, including models built from realized losses alone.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter choices can strongly affect reinforcement learning performance, but finding good settings is expensive. Population Based Training addresses this by adapting both model weights and hyperparameters during a single run involving multiple agents. The paper identifies a remaining weakness: random exploration heuristics provide no theoretical efficiency guarantees and can demand a large population.

Population-Based Bandits, or PB2, replaces that heuristic search with guidance from a probabilistic model. The model directs exploration of hyperparameter configurations within a population-based training process. The authors present PB2 as the first provably efficient algorithm of this style, giving theoretical grounding to how the search allocates its effort.

The practical aim is to discover strong configurations using far fewer agents than typically required by Population Based Training. Reinforcement learning experiments show that PB2 achieves high performance with a modest computational budget. These findings matter for settings where running a large training population is prohibitive: the reported improvements make online tuning more accessible without requiring a separate exhaustive search over configurations.
neurips-2020-provably-efficient-online-h.tldr: PB2 uses probabilistic search to make population-based hyperparameter tuning provably efficient and effective with smaller computational budgets.

paragraphs: Standard self-attention has a computational cost that grows quadratically with input length, making long inputs difficult to handle. Sparse Adaptive Connection, or SAC, represents the input sequence as a graph. Attention takes place only between nodes connected by edges, making the connection pattern a central part of how the model processes information.

SAC learns these attention edges to improve task performance instead of relying on a predefined structure. This lets it select salient nodes and reduce the quadratic complexity associated with unrestricted attention. The authors also show that earlier self-attention variants can be expressed as special cases, positioning SAC as a broader framework for choosing attention structure.

Experiments cover neural machine translation, language modeling, graph representation learning, and image classification. SAC is competitive with state-of-the-art models while substantially reducing memory use in the reported evaluations. The results support learning sparse connections as a way to preserve useful task performance across several applications while reducing the resources consumed by attention.
neurips-2020-sac-accelerating-and-struct.tldr: SAC learns sparse attention connections, reducing memory costs while remaining competitive across language, graph, and image tasks.

paragraphs: Neural networks are nonlinear models trained on nonconvex objectives, but those properties need not make every stage of learning equally complicated. This paper studies the beginning of training. For a class of well-behaved input distributions, it proves that training a simple linear model on the inputs can mimic the early learning dynamics of a two-layer fully connected network.

The analysis compares the Neural Tangent Kernel with an affine transformation of the data kernel and bounds their difference in spectral norm. This supplies a mathematical basis for the early linear approximation. Unlike many analyses using the Neural Tangent Kernel, the result does not require disproportionately wide networks.

The authors also argue that similar early simplicity can occur in deeper networks and convolutional architectures, and provide empirical verification of that extension. The time restriction is central: networks may leave the kernel regime later in training. The findings therefore describe an initially simple learning phase while allowing later behavior to develop beyond the approximation used to explain that phase.
neurips-2020-the-surprising-simplicity-o.tldr: Under suitable input-distribution conditions, a linear model can mimic a two-layer network's early training dynamics without requiring extreme width.

paragraphs: Unbalanced Sobolev Descent, or USD, transforms a source distribution toward a target whose total mass may differ. It represents distributions with particles and changes both their positions and their weights. This accommodates situations where matching distributions requires more than moving a fixed amount of mass from one location to another.

The method introduces the Sobolev-Fisher discrepancy and uses its witness function to guide two operations. An advection step moves particles along gradients, while a reaction step adjusts their mass. The latter can also be interpreted as particle birth and death. The paper connects these operations to transport equations and the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric.

With a witness estimated in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the authors prove asymptotic convergence in maximum mean discrepancy under mild assumptions and in the infinite-particle limit. They also develop two neural versions, using either weight updates or particle birth and death. Synthetic examples show faster transport than previous particle descent methods, and a biological application matches developmental stages of differentiating cell populations using single-cell RNA profiles.
neurips-2020-unbalanced-sobolev-descent-.tldr: USD matches distributions by moving particles and changing their mass, with conditional asymptotic guarantees and applications to cell development.

paragraphs: Explaining one prediction and explaining a feature's overall contribution are different interpretability tasks. This paper focuses on the latter, defining global feature importance through predictive power. The guiding question is how much each input feature contributes to useful prediction across the problem, rather than how it affects only one particular model output.

The authors distinguish model-based and universal notions of predictive power and organize feature attribution within a framework of additive importance measures. This framework unifies numerous existing methods. They then introduce SAGE, a model-agnostic approach that quantifies predictive power while accounting for feature interactions, recognizing that the usefulness of one feature can depend on other available features.

Experiments show that SAGE can be computed efficiently and assigns more accurate importance values than the compared methods. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: it provides a common basis for relating feature-importance methods and an estimator designed to reflect interacting contributions. Its global perspective makes the resulting importance values about overall predictive usefulness rather than isolated explanations of individual cases.
neurips-2020-understanding-global-featur.tldr: SAGE measures global feature importance through predictive power while accounting for interactions among features.
